messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaleo Manoa had built a life around calm procedures, checklists, and the expectation that every door, latch, and cockpit protocol would hold. As a 53-year-old airline pilot from an Oceanian background, married and usually known by colleagues as steady under pressure, he had once prided himself on being the man who stayed composed when others panicked. That changed after the period of detention and torture that he described only in fragments at first: a dark room, the scrape of a chair, the sour smell of sweat and damp concrete, and the terror of not knowing when the next blow would come. What made the memory so potent for him was not only what happened, but how vividly it still returned. When he tried to speak of it, the scene came back like a row of photographs he could not control, each detail fixed and clinical in its clarity, and sometimes the smell of that place seemed to arrive with it, sudden and exact, enough to make him stop mid-sentence. On those occasions he became so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to shut down the conversation and stare at the floor until the wave passed.

In the months after the trauma, Kaleo found that certain moments in ordinary life opened the door to that same inner collapse. A child crying in the terminal, a crowded gate area pressing too close around him, or the sight of someone openly misbehaving at work or in public could jolt him into the same state of alertness he had known in captivity. Those triggers mattered because they carried echoes of helplessness and loss of control, and once they struck, his mind immediately reached for the old images. A crying passenger or a packed boarding line could suddenly make the room feel dangerous, as though he were back in the presence of unpredictable people and unable to protect himself. He had come to believe that even a small breach in order could be the first sign of something worse.

The memory itself fed that danger. When the photographs in his mind returned, with the smells and the helplessness attached, he was left shaken for hours, and afterward he found himself scanning the world for confirmation that harm was coming. He repeatedly checked doors and windows at home before bed, then checked them again, not because he thought he had forgotten, but because the silence after the locks clicked seemed unnatural to him. Unusual quiet made him feel that something dangerous was about to happen, and he would lie awake listening for footsteps or movement in the hallway. At work, in the cabin and around the airport, he watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him. He studied faces, hands, and tone with a vigilance that felt, to him, like common sense. In his mind, the memory was never far away, and its intensity made the present feel precarious; the more the images and smells flooded back, the more certain he became that danger could be hiding in any pause, any closed door, any strange stillness.

That constant sense of threat, in turn, shaped what he noticed and how he moved through the world. Kaleo began avoiding crowded places whenever he could, arriving early or late to appointments so he would not have to stand in a thick, shifting line. He chose quieter routes through the airport and sat away from groups in crew rooms and waiting areas, partly to keep his distance from the pressure of bodies and partly because he felt he needed to see people before they saw him. Yet those efforts did not bring relief for long. When a terminal became dense with travelers or a child’s crying rose nearby, the same alarm would flare again, and he would search faces, exits, and corners with renewed intensity. The more he scanned for threat, the more quickly ordinary scenes seemed to confirm it, and the more tightly his life narrowed around what felt safe enough to endure.

Over time, his marriage carried the strain of all this vigilance. His wife noticed how often he got up at night to recheck locks and how easily he became distant after hearing a cry in public or seeing rude, reckless behavior. Kaleo hated how irrational it looked from the outside, but he could not shake the conviction that if he stayed alert enough he might prevent a repeat of what he had survived. He sought help only when he realized he was dreading layovers, avoiding crowded spaces on days off, and coming home so keyed up that he could barely sit through dinner. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming permanently trapped in the posture of someone waiting for an attack, and what he most hoped for was to feel safe enough again that a quiet room, a locked door, or another person’s tears would no longer feel like the beginning of something terrible.
